objective: Decide whether an arithmetic mean is meaningful from the scale and meaning of a variable.
Classify variables by measurement level, including numeric identifiers that are labels rather than quantities.
Choose defensible measures of center for variables with different measurement levels and distributions.
Calculate and compare the effect of an extreme value on the mean.
Sort two groups, calculate their medians, and interpret the comparison.
Calculate mean and median, recover a missing value from a known mean, and examine outlier sensitivity.
Calculate a pooled median and explain how replacements at different ranks affect it.
Calculate mean, mode, corrected sample variance, sample standard deviation, and range.
Show why equal means do not imply comparable distributions by comparing spread and shape.
Apply a linear transformation to a mean, variance, and standard deviation.
Standardize observations with z scores and verify the transformed mean and standard deviation.
Compare alternative graphical presentations of the same data and separate numerical change from visual impression.
Diagnose graphical choices that exaggerate a trend and specify a defensible repair.
Construct and jointly interpret a histogram and boxplot.
Construct histograms with different bin widths or origins and compare the resulting shapes.
Use sequential conditional multiplication for success through several stages and failure at the final stage.
Calculate joint probabilities for independent events.
Use a two-way table to examine conditional probabilities, joint probability, independence, and disjointness.
Apply Bayes' theorem under changing prevalence and explain the base-rate effect.
Calculate expectation and variance and represent a discrete distribution with its PMF and CDF.
Calculate exact binomial probabilities and check the model conditions.
Calculate an upper binomial tail efficiently through its complement.
Distinguish a discrete probability mass function from a continuous density.
Calculate lower-tail, upper-tail, and interval probabilities under the standard normal model.
Standardize a nonstandard normal variable and calculate probabilities.
Find inverse standard-normal quantiles from cumulative probabilities.
Calculate the mean and standard error of a sampling distribution and explain how variance and sample size affect precision.
Calculate interval probabilities under a general normal model by standardizing both boundaries.
Distinguish population, sampling frame, achieved sample, parameter, and statistic and diagnose selection and nonresponse bias.
Diagnose coverage error in a broad percentage claim based on a restricted profile frame.
Diagnose survivorship bias by identifying observable cases and outcome-dependent missing cases.
Formulate null and alternative hypotheses and interpret Type I and Type II errors in context.
Calculate sample estimates and an estimated standard error and name their population targets.
Construct known-sigma confidence intervals across several sample sizes.
Explain and calculate how confidence level, sample size, and variability affect interval width.
Carry out a one-sided z test and identify the decision error that remains possible.
Formulate and carry out a two-sided z test.
Distinguish p-value and power, calculate both, and plan a sample size for target power.
Carry out a two-sided test and connect the result with interval estimation and practical size.
Interpret t quantiles, symmetry, degrees of freedom, and convergence toward the normal distribution.
Choose and carry out a one-sample t test when population variance is unknown.
Construct a one-sample t interval and use its duality with the matching two-sided test.
Identify independent samples and carry out a pooled two-sample t test under equal variance.
Calculate Pearson correlation and recognize that a near-zero coefficient can conceal nonlinear association.
Explain a third-variable account and the boundary between correlation and causation.
Calculate Pearson correlation, test a directional population correlation, and separate statistical from practical importance.
Assign ranks and calculate Spearman correlation.
Compare Pearson and Spearman correlation for a monotonic nonlinear pattern.
Calculate Spearman correlation with ties and reason about invariance under a positive linear transformation.
Diagnose causal, third-variable, measurement, sampling, and aggregate-to-individual problems in association claims.
Read a scatterplot, calculate least-squares coefficients from raw sums, interpret them, and make an in-range prediction.
Move from means, standard deviations, and covariance to correlation, a regression line, and a point prediction.
Distinguish and interpret unstandardized and standardized slopes.
Locate coefficients in output, interpret signs and units, and compare standardized slopes.
Calculate regression coefficients and obtain R-squared from explained and total sums of squares.
Test a regression slope, interpret its p-value, construct a confidence interval, and connect interval and test.
State and test the simple-regression model hypothesis through R-squared.
Combine slope inference, R-squared, model testing, and careful substantive interpretation when evidence is weak.
Use graphical evidence to distinguish a plausible residual distribution from an obvious normality violation.
Compare original-data and residual plots for a sound linear model, nonlinearity, and unequal residual variance.
Calculate a partial correlation from residuals and verify it with the three-correlation formula.
Explain the difference between bivariate and partial correlation with a conceptual shared-variance visual.
Read a multiple-regression equation and output and interpret conditional coefficients, coefficient tests, and model fit.
Compare a nested model sequence with R-squared, adjusted R-squared, and an explicit decrement test.
Distinguish the global F test from individual coefficient t tests and their null hypotheses.
Use semipartial correlations and incremental R-squared in a forward model-building argument.
Carry out sequential forward comparison by AIC, trace the AIC path, state the final model, and interpret it cautiously.
Construct k minus one dummy indicators and identify the reference category.
Interpret a binary group indicator and quantitative predictor in an additive common-slope model.
Change the reference category and verify that fitted group relationships remain unchanged.
Construct, calculate, graph, and interpret a group-by-quantitative-predictor interaction.
State the question and hypotheses answered by one-way ANOVA.
Plot group means, calculate the complete sum-of-squares partition, and carry out a one-way F test.
Reconstruct a one-way ANOVA table, state hypotheses, identify balance, and separate association from causal design.
Compare simple pairwise contrasts with a pooled complex contrast.
Count all pairwise comparisons and calculate a Bonferroni per-test threshold.
Define each comparison family honestly and distinguish prospective planning from data-dependent selection.
Compare candidate trend weights, sketch them, repair an invalid contrast, and test the valid linear trend.
Complete cell and marginal means, reconstruct factorial tests, and interpret a means plot with interaction.
Distinguish fixed and random factors, state the population target, and calculate a one-way random-factor ICC.
Assess sphericity from variances and correlations, test condition and person effects, calculate ICC, and apply Greenhouse-Geisser correction.
